attestations.notes: Proof 1.1–4.1 read: nonempty first-order domain supplies a set; Separation with z != z produces the empty subset; Extensionality gives uniqueness.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: nonemptiness supplies B in x, Separation inside B gives exactly the universal membership class, and Extensionality removes dependence on B. The empty indexing set is excluded.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: the weak Power Set carrier is narrowed by Separation to exactly the subsets; Extensionality proves uniqueness, including x empty.
Proof 1.1–2.1 read: membership conditions establish all five small-family identities, including empty union; intersections are used only for nonempty singleton/pair families.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: both coordinates lie in A union B, their singleton/pair lie in its power set, and the Kuratowski pair lies in the double power set. Empty factors make the premises vacuous.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: both implications use extensional membership; the a=b and a!=b cases include collapsed pairs and yield the singleton specialization.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: unordered-pair equality gives the aligned or swapped alternatives; each forces both coordinate equalities, including collapsed singleton pairs. Reverse implication is substitution.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: Kuratowski coordinates lie in the double union of R; Separation there constructs domain/range with exact existential membership, including R empty.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: Separation in one inductive carrier defines membership in every inductive set; zero/successor closure and two inclusions prove existence, minimality and uniqueness without a class intersection.
Proof 1.1–5.1 read: the assumed zero/successor closure makes S inductive, hence minimal omega lies in S; Separation gives the stated property form.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction proves transitivity and irreflexivity together. In the successor self-membership alternatives, transitivity or successor equality forces n in n.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: intersect closed subsets of N times A, prove totality by induction, delete an extraneous zero/successor pair using P1/P2 to force uniqueness, then induct on equality for uniqueness of g. No choice of a family of values is needed.
Proof 1.1–2.1 read: induction gives P3; successor contains n, giving P1; equal successors with unequal coordinates force a forbidden self-membership by transitivity, giving P2.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: recursion with A=N, initial m and successor supplies each unique total s_m, whose equations define the total binary addition operation.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c proves associativity using only the zero clause and two successor-recursion substitutions.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n proves the left zero identity; the right zero identity is the defining recursion clause.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on the second argument establishes the left-successor addition law using the defining right-successor recursion in both directions.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n uses left zero identity and left-successor addition to close the commutativity step.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on the common right summand uses successor injectivity to reduce each equality to the preceding summand; zero is the base case.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the subset of zero-or-successor naturals contains zero and is successor closed, so induction yields the claimed dichotomy.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: cancellation, commutativity and nonzero-successor form exclude both strict directions simultaneously; induction handles the three predecessor comparisons, with a=0 singled out in the last case.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: additive witnesses give reflexivity/transitivity; nonzero-successor and P1 show a zero sum has zero summands, enabling antisymmetry by cancellation; trichotomy supplies totality.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: rewrite a nonzero additive witness as a successor for the forward implication, and use cancellation plus P1 for strictness in the reverse. Opposite strict inequalities then exclude intermediate k.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: existential coordinates put each relation pair in dom R times ran R; ordered-pair uniqueness supplies the forward containment criterion and the reverse follows from the same witnesses, including R empty.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: inverse and composite pairs are bounded by the appropriate domain/range products before Separation; restriction is separated directly inside R. The construction includes empty relations.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: P1 supplies the zero base and successor injectivity converts a successor fixed point to a forbidden predecessor fixed point.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: induction first proves every member of each n is natural; discreteness and additive linear order identify membership with strict order by two inductions. Transitivity and irreflexivity then give subset order and the zero/successor consequences without ordinals.

Proof 1.1–7.1 read: codomain transposition normalizes the top value of an alleged injection, so its restriction contradicts induction. The four consequences use restrictions, trichotomy or inverses; the proper-subset case explicitly handles n=0 and selects only one missing element, with no choice axiom.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: assuming no least element makes the initial segments disjoint from S; discreteness closes this property under successor and induction forces S empty, contradicting its hypothesis.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: recursion with initial zero and x->x+m constructs each total p_m; its unique recursion equations define multiplication on all natural pairs.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: the same additive gap witness is transported in either direction by associativity/commutativity and cancellation. The strict equivalence also uses cancellation to reflect inequality.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the right unit is a direct recursion calculation; joint induction gives left zero and left unit, including the base n=0.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c proves left distributivity; the separate complete induction on n proves successor-left multiplication using only associative/commutative addition and the two recursion clauses.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: multiplication induction uses left zero at the base and the previously proved successor-left law to close the symmetry step.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c reduces the multiplication successor equation to left distributivity; the zero base is explicit.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: under two nonzero factors, write each as a successor; multiplication then becomes a successor by addition recursion, so P1 excludes zero. This proves exactly the contrapositive.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: right distributivity transports the order gap d to d*k; for strictness both d and k are nonzero, so no zero divisors and additive cancellation exclude equality. k=0 is allowed only in the weak inequality.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: adding the two representative equivalence equations establishes the summed pair relation, while swapping the first equation establishes negation independence.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: factor both cross-sums using the representative equality a+bprime=b+aprime; symmetry of the multiplication formula handles the second representative, then compose the two equalities.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: all ring axioms are verified on quotient representatives; the associative multiplication expansion gives the same four terms in each coordinate, distributivity matches coordinatewise, and additive inverses are zero classes.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: translation-invariant natural order proves independence of integer representatives, transitivity and additive compatibility. For positive products the two positive natural gaps give ac+bd=(ad+bc)+k*m, with k*m nonzero.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: distributivity yields 0*a=0*a+0*a; additive cancellation of the common term yields 0*a=0, for every field element including a=0.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the field difference identities show translation invariance; adding two positive differences and cone closure prove addition of strict inequalities.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: distributivity and zero multiplication show each singly negated product is the additive inverse of ab; inverse uniqueness and double negation give the doubly negated product.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: positive-cone product closure proves the three sign cases; difference identities give forward monotonicity/reversal and trichotomy excludes equality or reversed comparisons for both converses. The scalar is explicitly nonzero through its sign.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: for nonzero a the positive or negative cases are exhaustive; cone closure and (-a)*(-a)=a*a make its square positive. No conclusion of strict positivity is made at a=0.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: 1 is nonzero by field axioms, so the square lemma at 1 and 1*1=1 prove positivity.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: a positive inverse cannot be zero or negative because its product is positive 1; multiplying a<b by positive a_inverse*b_inverse reverses the reciprocal comparison. Both a,b are positive.
Proof 1.1–2.1 read: associative abelian-group calculations prove identities and inverse uniqueness; multiplicative inverses are restricted to nonzero x in the final statement.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the four sign cases use positive-product closure and ring negation to exclude a zero product; distributivity reduces cancellation with z!=0 to that result.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: each quotient operation preserves the cross-product relation by explicit integer ring expansions; input denominators are nonzero and the cited rational-operation interface supplies the admissible product denominators.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: fixed-representative computations verify every field law. Distributivity compares the two representatives by the common nonzero denominator factor; a nonzero class has nonzero numerator and inverse (b,a), and 1 differs from 0.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: all representatives have positive denominators. Positive integer scaling proves representative independence, transitivity and additive compatibility; positive numerator/denominator products give the positive cone. The cancellation of d and f_squared uses their positivity.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: evaluate e*f using each one-sided identity; this gives equality and both uniqueness consequences without associativity.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: h*(g*hprime)=(h*g)*hprime uses associativity and both identity laws to identify left/right inverses. The one-sided conclusion is explicitly conditional on g already invertible.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction gives positivity of repeated 1 and successor increase; iterating the strict increase gives injectivity. Separate inductions prove additive and multiplicative compatibility, with m,n>=1 and the zero convention stated.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: pair equivalence immediately proves injectivity, arithmetic and order preservation for n->[(n,0)]. A nonnegative integer has a natural gap k between its two coordinates, yielding precisely that image and uniqueness.
